title: Reform begins
hookLine: German Jews change services: sermons, organs, the vernacular

cards: A Sabbath morning in a German town. Jewish families walk in to pray, and the room sounds different. There is an organ.
A choir sings. Some prayers are in German, the language these families now speak at home and at work. Then a man stands and gives a sermon, in German, polished and earnest.
Some are moved to tears; for once they understand every word. Others walk out shaken; to them this is no longer the synagogue of their parents. Today, Reform begins.

teach.b: The new citizens of yesterday's story faced a real worry.

Their children were learning German, going to German schools, entering German professions, and some were drifting away from Judaism altogether, finding the synagogue long, hard to follow, and out of step with the rest of their week.
A group of German Jews decided the answer was to change the service itself.
A layman named Israel Jacobson built a house of prayer with an organ and held services with German hymns and German sermons.
In Hamburg, a congregation opened a temple with its own new prayer book: shorter, partly in German, and with changes to some prayers about the return to Zion.
They wanted worship that was dignified, understandable and modern. The organ became a symbol of the whole fight.
Supporters could point to Psalm one hundred fifty, as the King James Bible renders it: "Praise him with stringed instruments and organs."
Opponents answered that playing an instrument on the Sabbath breaks the Sabbath, that the organ imitated the church, and that the prayers were not anyone's to rewrite.

Traditional rabbis published rulings against the Hamburg prayer book. The reformers feared losing the young to the world. The traditionalists feared losing the prayers their parents had said, word for word.
The Reform movement grew out of these first changes, and so did new ways of defending tradition, which we'll meet tomorrow.
And the question the organ raised, what may change in a service and who decides, would be argued in synagogue after synagogue.

how: Reform synagogues today commonly hold services that mix Hebrew with the local language and include instrumental music, while Orthodox synagogues keep a traditional Hebrew service without instruments on Shabbat.

games.q: you're Israel Jacobson. young Jews find the synagogue long and hard to follow, and some are drifting away. what do you do?
o: change nothing; the young will come back.
build a house of prayer with an organ, German hymns and German sermons.
games.why: he built a house of prayer with an organ and German hymns and sermons, and the fight over it began at once.

practice: Think of something that changed around you, a family tradition done a new way, a community that modernized, and let yourself feel both sides: what was gained, what was lost, who welcomed it and who walked out quietly.
You don't have to decide who was right; just hold the tears of the one who finally understood and the shock of the one who no longer recognized the room.

wordCard.voice: Jacobson. The layman who built the first Reform-style house of prayer, with an organ, German hymns, and sermons the young could understand. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: tears, and people walking out. Under each side's argument was a fear of losing something. See you tomorrow.
